lines.text: High in the Pyrenees, between France and Spain, lies a tiny country with two princes and very old ways. This is the story of Andorra.
Andorra's story as a country begins in 1278, in a set of mountain valleys that both a bishop and a count wanted to rule.
That year they agreed to share it. The Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix became co-princes, an arrangement that, in its way, still holds today.
In 1580 the Casa de la Vall was built, the old stone house where Andorra's parliament would meet for centuries.
Oscar Ribas Reig, born in 1936, would become Andorra's first head of government, in 1982.
Joan Enric Vives, born in 1949, would become Bishop of Urgell, and with it co-prince of Andorra, in 2003.
Xavier Espot Zamora, born in 1979, would lead the government from 2019.
In 1993 the people approved a constitution, making Andorra a modern parliamentary co-principality, and that same year it joined the United Nations.
Its parliament, the General Council, first met in 1419, making it one of the oldest in Europe, and now it had a modern charter at last.
Seven centuries on, Andorra still has its two princes and its mountain valleys.
